breakfast.name: Halim (Wheat and Meat Porridge)
instructions: Soak wheat berries overnight — they need to be very soft
Cook wheat and meat together in water for 3-4 hours, stirring often
The wheat breaks down completely into a thick, smooth porridge
The meat shreds into the wheat — they become one texture
The consistency should be like thick oatmeal — smooth and homogeneous
Serve in a bowl, top with melted butter, cinnamon, and sugar
The sweet-savory combination is the signature — butter, sugar, and meat
Halim is Iran's cold-weather breakfast — nourishing and warming
Sold from street carts and specialty shops in every Iranian city
The slow cooking transforms simple ingredients into something deeply comforting
breakfast.description: Iran's ancient wheat-and-meat porridge — wheat berries and lamb cooked for hours until they merge into a thick, smooth, nourishing bowl topped with butter, cinnamon, and sugar. The sweet-savory finish is uniquely Persian. Halim is cold-weather comfort and has been eaten in Iran for thousands of years.

breakfast.name: Naan-o Paneer-o Sabzi (Bread, Cheese, Herbs)
ingredients: Sangak or barbari bread (fresh from the bakery)
Fresh herbs: basil, tarragon, mint, chives, radish tops
instructions: Buy fresh bread from the neighborhood bakery — sangak (pebble-baked) or barbari
Arrange cheese, herbs, walnuts, and radishes on a plate
Tear bread, take a piece of cheese, wrap with herbs and a walnut
The combination of fresh herbs, salty cheese, and warm bread is perfect
Iranians eat more fresh herbs per capita than almost any country
The herb plate (sabzi khordan) appears at every Iranian meal
This breakfast is about the freshness — nothing is cooked
Serve with hot sweet tea — the tea is essential
This is the daily Iranian breakfast — simple, fresh, ancient
breakfast.description: The Iranian breakfast table — warm fresh bread, white cheese, and a mountain of fresh herbs (basil, tarragon, mint, chives). Iranians eat more fresh herbs than almost any other nation. The 'bread-cheese-herb wrap' technique and the sheer volume of fresh herbs are viral.

breakfast.name: Adasi (Lentil Soup)
instructions: Cook lentils in water with turmeric until very soft — 25-30 min
Meanwhile caramelize onion until deep golden
Add tomato paste, cook briefly
Mash lentils partially — some whole, some smooth
Top with caramelized onion
Squeeze lime juice or sprinkle golpar (angelica powder — uniquely Iranian)
Serve with warm flatbread for dipping and scooping
Adasi is Iran's comfort food — cheap, warming, satisfying
Every university student and every grandmother makes adasi
breakfast.description: Iran's everyday lentil soup — turmeric-golden lentils topped with deeply caramelized onion and a squeeze of lime. Cheap, warming, and universally loved from students to grandmothers. The caramelized onion crown and the golden turmeric color are the visual hooks.

breakfast.name: Kaleh Pacheh (Head and Trotters Soup)
instructions: Clean sheep head and trotters thoroughly
Boil overnight or for 6+ hours — very low heat
The collagen from the bones creates an incredibly rich, gelatinous broth
The meat falls off the bones — tongue, cheek, brain are all eaten
Season with turmeric, cinnamon, salt
Serve in bowls with lime juice squeezed in
Eat with sangak bread — tear and dip
This is a 4 AM food — specialty shops open before dawn
Iranians eat kaleh pacheh as a very early breakfast or after a long night
The rich, gelatinous broth is considered deeply restorative
breakfast.description: Iran's pre-dawn soup — sheep head and trotters simmered overnight into a rich, gelatinous broth. Specialty shops open at 4 AM to serve this restorative bowl. The extreme nose-to-tail tradition, the collagen-rich broth, and the 4 AM eating culture are viral.

lunch.name: Ghormeh Sabzi (Herb Stew)
ingredients: Fresh herbs: parsley, cilantro, chives, fenugreek leaves (lots — a mountain of herbs)
Dried limes (limoo amani — the signature ingredient)
instructions: The herb ratio is extreme — buy more herbs than you think is reasonable, then buy more
Wash and finely chop ALL herbs — this takes time but is non-negotiable
Fry herbs in oil until dark green and fragrant — 20-30 min
Brown meat with turmeric and onion
Add fried herbs to the meat with kidney beans
Add dried limes — pierce them so the sour juice releases into the stew
Add water, simmer 2+ hours until meat is tender and stew is thick
The dried limes give a unique sour-bitter depth that nothing else can replicate
The stew should be very dark green, thick, and intensely herby
Serve over fluffy Persian rice — the stew-on-rice combination is sacred
lunch.description: Iran's national dish — a dark green herb stew with lamb, kidney beans, and dried limes, served over rice. The sheer volume of fresh herbs (parsley, cilantro, fenugreek) and the unique dried lime sourness create a flavor found nowhere else. Voted Iran's favorite food in every poll. The 'that's how many herbs?!' reaction is perpetually viral.

lunch.name: Zereshk Polo ba Morgh (Barberry Rice with Chicken)
ingredients: Sugar (tiny bit — to balance barberry tartness)
instructions: Cook chicken with onion, turmeric, salt until tender
Make perfect Persian rice: parboil, drain, layer back in pot with oil, steam with a towel under the lid
The tahdig (crispy bottom layer) is the most important part — golden, crunchy, coveted
Sauté barberries briefly in butter with a pinch of sugar — they burn easily
Dissolve saffron in hot water — the golden color is essential
Mix saffron water into a portion of rice — this creates the golden rice
Serve: white rice on the platter, golden saffron rice scattered on top, barberries over everything
The red-gold-white color combination is stunning
The chicken goes alongside or underneath the rice
The tahdig gets its own plate — it's the prize, and there's always a fight for it
lunch.description: Iran's most beautiful rice dish — fluffy white rice jeweled with ruby-red barberries and streaked with golden saffron, served with tender chicken. The tahdig (coveted crispy rice bottom) causes family arguments over who gets the biggest piece. The color palette and the tahdig fight are the most viral elements of Persian food.

lunch.name: Tahchin (Saffron Rice Cake)
instructions: Mix parboiled rice with yogurt, egg yolks, saffron, butter, salt
Layer in a pot: half the yogurt-rice mixture on the bottom
Add a layer of shredded chicken or lamb
Top with remaining yogurt-rice
Cook on very low heat for 60-90 min — the bottom must form a golden crust
The entire bottom and sides should become a crispy, golden, saffron-stained shell
Flip onto a plate — the reveal of the golden crust is the moment
The inside is tender rice with meat; the outside is crispy saffron yogurt crust
Garnish with barberries and saffron rice
This is the most architectural Persian rice dish — it's a rice cake, not a pilaf
lunch.description: Iran's saffron rice cake — rice mixed with yogurt, egg, and saffron, layered with chicken, and slow-cooked until the entire exterior becomes a golden, crispy shell. The dramatic flip-onto-plate reveal shows a perfect golden dome. Tahchin is Persian rice engineering at its peak and the flip reveal is viral.

lunch.name: Fesenjan (Pomegranate Walnut Stew)
instructions: Toast and finely grind walnuts — they become the body of the stew
Sauté onion, add turmeric, brown chicken or duck
Add ground walnuts and enough water to create a thick sauce
Add pomegranate molasses — generous, the stew should be deeply tart-sweet
Simmer on very low heat for 2+ hours — the walnut oil releases slowly
The stew turns dark brown-purple from the pomegranate
Adjust sweet-sour balance with sugar and more pomegranate molasses
The consistency should be thick, rich, and glossy from the walnut oils
Serve over Persian rice
Fesenjan is celebration food — weddings, Shab-e Yalda (winter solstice), Nowruz
lunch.description: Iran's pomegranate-walnut stew — ground walnuts and pomegranate molasses create a dark, glossy, tart-sweet sauce for chicken or duck. Fesenjan is served at weddings and Nowruz. The unique pomegranate-walnut combination exists nowhere else in world cuisine, making fesenjan one of the most viral and distinctive Persian dishes.

lunch.name: Joojeh Kabab (Saffron Chicken Kabab)
instructions: Marinate chicken in saffron water, onion juice, lemon juice, yogurt — overnight
Thread onto flat metal skewers — the flat shape keeps the meat from spinning
Grill over hot charcoal — Iranian kabab is always charcoal-grilled
Baste with butter and saffron water while grilling
Grill grilled tomatoes alongside — they char and soften
The chicken should be golden-saffron colored, charred at edges, juicy inside
Serve over rice or with flatbread
Sprinkle sumac (tart red powder) over the rice
Squeeze grilled tomato over the rice — it becomes the sauce
Kabab and rice is Iran's most universal meal
lunch.description: Iran's saffron chicken kabab — marinated in saffron, lemon, and yogurt, charcoal-grilled until golden. The butter basting and the saffron color create chicken kabab that's distinctly Persian. Served with rice and grilled tomato, with sumac dust. The saffron-golden color on the charcoal grill is the viral image.

dinner.name: Chelo Kabab Koobideh (Ground Meat Kabab)
ingredients: Ground lamb (or lamb-beef mix — at least 20% fat)
instructions: Mix ground meat with grated onion (squeezed completely dry — moisture makes kabab fall apart)
Season with salt and pepper — keep it simple
Knead the meat vigorously — the proteins bind, making it stick to the skewer
Shape onto wide flat skewers — long, thin cylinders
The meat must grip the skewer — if it falls off, the kneading wasn't enough
Grill over very hot charcoal — 3-4 min per side
Baste with saffron butter
The kabab should be charred outside, juicy inside
Serve on a bed of saffron-streaked rice with grilled tomato and raw onion
Slide kabab off skewer directly onto the rice — the sizzle is the moment
dinner.description: Iran's most iconic kabab — ground lamb kneaded until it grips a flat skewer, charcoal-grilled with saffron butter, slid onto fluffy rice. Koobideh is Iran's everyday luxury. The skewer technique (making ground meat stick without falling) and the sizzle-onto-rice moment are perpetually viral.

dinner.name: Baghali Polo ba Mahicheh (Dill-Fava Rice with Lamb Shank)
ingredients: Fava beans (broad beans — fresh or frozen)
instructions: Braise lamb shanks with onion and turmeric for 2-3 hours until falling off the bone
Parboil rice, drain
Mix rice with chopped dill and fava beans
Layer in pot with oil/butter on the bottom for tahdig
Steam with towel under lid — 45-60 min
The dill and fava turn the rice green-speckled and fragrant
Dissolve saffron, drizzle over a portion of rice — golden saffron rice on top
The tahdig with dill and fava embedded is the most coveted piece
Serve: pile rice on platter, place lamb shank on top
The fall-off-the-bone lamb on the green-gold rice is a masterpiece of plating
dinner.description: Iran's spring celebration rice — basmati studded with fresh dill and fava beans, served with braised lamb shank so tender it falls off the bone. The green-gold-brown color palette and the falling-apart lamb on fragrant rice make baghali polo one of the most beautiful dishes in Persian cuisine.

dinner.name: Kashk-e Bademjan (Eggplant and Whey Dip)
ingredients: Kashk (fermented whey — tangy, thick, uniquely Iranian)
instructions: Roast or fry eggplant until completely soft and collapsed
Mash the eggplant — it should be smooth
Caramelize onion very deeply — dark brown, sweet
Fry garlic separately until golden
Add kashk (fermented whey) to the mashed eggplant — mix well
The kashk gives a unique tangy, creamy, slightly funky flavor
Top with caramelized onion, fried garlic, fried dried mint, walnuts
Serve warm with flatbread for scooping
Kashk is an ancient Persian preserved dairy — it tastes like nothing else
The toppings (onion, garlic, mint, walnut) on the creamy base are the visual hook
dinner.description: Iran's eggplant dip — roasted eggplant mixed with kashk (fermented whey, an ancient Persian ingredient), topped with caramelized onion, fried garlic, and fried mint. Kashk gives a unique funky-tangy flavor found nowhere outside Persian cuisine. The dramatic topping display is viral.

dinner.name: Khoresh-e Gheymeh (Split Pea and Lamb Stew)
instructions: Brown lamb with onion and turmeric
Add tomato paste — fry until dark
Add split peas, dried limes (pierced), cinnamon, water
Simmer 90 min until lamb is tender and split peas are soft
The dried limes give the same unique sourness as ghormeh sabzi
The stew should be thick, golden-orange, and rich
Make fried potato matchsticks: julienne potatoes, fry until crispy and golden
Top each serving with a mountain of fried potato sticks
Serve over rice with saffron
The fried potato topping is the defining feature of gheymeh
dinner.description: Iran's split pea stew — lamb and yellow split peas in a tomato-lime broth, crowned with a mountain of crispy fried potato matchsticks. The dramatic potato-stick topping and the dried-lime sourness make gheymeh one of the most distinctive and photogenic Persian stews.

dinner.name: Abgoosht (Dizi — Stone Pot Stew)
instructions: Combine everything in a stone pot (dizi pot) or regular pot
Add water, bring to simmer
Cook for 2+ hours — the lamb must be completely tender
The magic: remove the broth (ab) into bowls — drink it as soup with bread
The remaining solids (goosht) are MASHED together with a pestle into a paste
The paste is eaten with flatbread — tear bread, scoop paste, eat
Two courses from one pot: broth soup first, then mashed meat-bean paste
The mashing is the iconic moment — a heavy pestle pounds everything together
This is Iran's oldest surviving stew — the stone pot method is ancient
Dizi shops are a beloved restaurant category in Iran
dinner.description: Iran's two-course-from-one-pot stew — first drink the broth as soup, then mash the remaining meat, beans, and potato into a paste eaten with bread. The stone-pot cooking and the dramatic pestle-mashing step make abgoosht one of the most unique dining experiences in the world. The mashing video is perpetually viral.

snacks.name: Ash Reshteh (Noodle Herb Soup)
ingredients: Herbs: parsley, cilantro, dill, chives, spinach
instructions: Cook all three legumes until tender
Finely chop the mountain of herbs — this is a LOT of herbs
Sauté herbs with turmeric until dark and fragrant
Add legumes and water — simmer into a thick soup
Add reshteh noodles — cook until soft, 10 min
The soup should be THICK — more stew than soup
Top with kashk (drizzled in artistic patterns), caramelized onion, fried garlic, fried mint
The toppings are essential — they add fat, tang, crunch, and aroma
Ash reshteh is Nowruz (Persian New Year) food
It's also the 'moving house' soup — made when starting something new
snacks.description: Iran's celebration noodle soup — thick with herbs, three kinds of legumes, and flat noodles, topped with kashk, caramelized onion, and fried mint. Made for Nowruz and new beginnings. The dramatic drizzled-kashk topping and the 'soup of new beginnings' tradition are deeply viral.

snacks.name: Kuku Sabzi (Herb Frittata)
ingredients: Fresh herbs: parsley, cilantro, dill, chives (massive amount — more herb than egg)
instructions: Finely chop ALL herbs — this is an herb dish with eggs, not an egg dish with herbs
Beat eggs, add herbs, walnuts, barberries, turmeric, baking powder
The ratio should be mostly green (herbs) with enough egg to hold it together
Pour into an oiled pan, cook on low heat until set — 15-20 min
Flip or finish under broiler — the top should be golden
Cut into wedges — the interior should be deep green
Serve warm, room temperature, or cold — all are traditional
Kuku sabzi is Nowruz (Persian New Year) essential — on every haft-sin table
The herb-to-egg ratio shocks people — it's green all the way through
snacks.description: Iran's herb frittata — more herbs than eggs, creating a deep-green, dense, fragrant wedge served at every Nowruz celebration. The extreme herb-to-egg ratio ('that's ALL herbs!') and the jewel-like barberries make kuku sabzi one of the most photogenic and viral Persian dishes.

snacks.name: Lavashak (Fruit Leather)
ingredients: Sour plums, sour cherries, or pomegranate (any tart fruit)
instructions: Blend fruit into a smooth purée
Spread very thin on a baking sheet or traditionally on a cloth in the sun
Dry in oven at very low heat (60-70°C) for 2-3 hours, or sun-dry for 1-2 days
The purée dehydrates into thin, flexible sheets of concentrated fruit
Roll up the sheets — they become fruit leather rolls
The flavor is intensely sour-sweet — concentrated fruit
Lavashak is Iran's universal snack — every child grows up eating it
The sour plum version is the most popular — tart, addictive, staining
Iranian snack culture revolves around sour flavors — Iranians love sour
Sold everywhere in plastic-wrapped rolls
snacks.description: Iran's fruit leather — tart fruit dried into thin, intensely sour-sweet sheets rolled up as snacks. Iranians love sour flavors more than almost any cuisine, and lavashak is the purest expression of that. The sour-face reaction and the rolling technique are viral Iranian snack content.

snacks.name: Falafel (Iranian Southern Style)
instructions: Soak chickpeas overnight — do NOT cook them, they must be raw
Grind chickpeas with herbs, onion, garlic, spices in a food processor
Add baking powder — this is what makes them fluffy inside
Shape into balls or patties
Deep fry until dark golden and crispy — 4-5 min
The outside should be deeply crunchy, the inside bright green and fluffy
Iranian falafel (from Khuzestan province) adds turmeric — the yellow tint is the tell
Served in flatbread with herbs, pickled vegetables, and hot sauce
Southern Iranian falafel culture rivals Lebanon and Egypt's — it's a serious falafel region
snacks.description: Southern Iranian falafel — the Khuzestan province version with turmeric creating a yellow-green interior. Iran's Arab-influenced south has a falafel culture that rivals Lebanon's. The turmeric addition and the 'raw chickpea to crunchy ball' transformation are the hooks.

desserts.name: Sholeh Zard (Saffron Rice Pudding)
instructions: Cook rice in water until very soft and broken down — 45 min
Add sugar, stir until dissolved
Add saffron dissolved in rose water — the pudding turns deep golden
Add butter — it enriches the texture
Cook until thick and pudding-like
Pour into a wide dish or individual bowls
Decorate with slivered almonds, cinnamon patterns, and pistachios
The decoration is traditional — geometric patterns in cinnamon are an art form
Let set — serve at room temperature or cold
Sholeh zard is made for religious occasions — Nazri (charitable food, vowed to be shared)
desserts.description: Iran's saffron rice pudding — golden with saffron, fragrant with rose water, decorated with cinnamon art patterns. Sholeh zard is made as nazri (food vowed to be given away), connecting dessert to generosity. The golden color, the cinnamon decoration art, and the charitable tradition are deeply viral.

desserts.name: Bastani Sonnati (Iranian Ice Cream)
ingredients: Salep (orchid root powder — the thickener that gives the chewy stretch)
instructions: Heat milk and cream with sugar
Add salep — this orchid-root powder gives the ice cream its famous stretchy, chewy texture
Add rose water and saffron — the flavor profile is floral-golden
Churn in an ice cream maker
Fold in chopped pistachios and chunks of frozen clotted cream
The clotted cream chunks don't fully melt — they create pockets of richness
The texture is stretchier and chewier than Western ice cream — salep is the secret
Scoop between two wafers for the classic Iranian presentation
Bastani sonnati is Iran's most beloved street food — the wafer sandwich
The stretch when you pull the wafer apart is the viral moment
desserts.description: Iran's traditional ice cream — saffron, rose water, pistachios, and chunks of frozen clotted cream in a base made chewy with salep (orchid root). The stretch when pulling apart the wafer sandwich is the most viral moment in Persian food. Bastani sonnati is unlike any Western ice cream.

desserts.name: Faloodeh (Rose Water Sorbet with Noodles)
ingredients: Thin rice noodles (vermicelli — frozen into the sorbet)
instructions: Make sugar syrup with rose water — let cool
Cook thin vermicelli noodles briefly, drain, cool
Mix noodles into the rose water syrup
Freeze, stirring occasionally to create a granita-like texture with noodle strands
The noodles freeze into icy strands — creating a unique texture
Serve in bowls, squeeze lime juice on top
Sprinkle with pistachios
The combination of icy-crunchy noodle strands with rose water and lime is unique
Faloodeh is one of the world's oldest frozen desserts — over 2000 years old
Shiraz (the city) claims to be the birthplace of faloodeh
desserts.description: Iran's 2000-year-old frozen dessert — thin rice noodles frozen in rose water syrup, served with lime juice. Possibly the world's oldest frozen dessert, predating Italian gelato by centuries. The icy noodle texture and the ancient-origin story make faloodeh perpetually viral.

desserts.name: Gaz (Persian Nougat)
ingredients: Gaz-angebin (manna — sap from a wild plant in Isfahan region)
instructions: Whip egg whites until stiff peaks
Boil sugar syrup to hard-ball stage
Add gaz-angebin (the manna sap that gives this nougat its name)
Slowly pour hot syrup into egg whites while whipping continuously
Add rose water, cardamom
Fold in pistachios
Pour into a mold lined with rice paper
Let set, cut into pieces
The texture is chewy-crispy, the flavor is rose-pistachio-floral
Gaz is Isfahan's most famous sweet — sold in ornate boxes as gifts
The manna ingredient comes from a wild plant found only in certain Iranian regions
desserts.description: Isfahan's legendary nougat — made with gaz-angebin (manna from a wild plant), egg whites, rose water, and pistachios. The rare manna ingredient, the rose-pistachio flavor, and Isfahan's reputation as Iran's most beautiful city make gaz the most prestigious Persian sweet.

drinks.name: Doogh (Yogurt Soda)
instructions: Mix yogurt with cold sparkling water — ratio about 1:1
Add salt — it should be noticeably salty
Add dried mint — generous
Add black pepper if desired
Stir or blend until frothy
Serve ice cold
Doogh is Iran's meal companion — drunk with every kabab, every rice dish
The salty-sour-minty combination is addictive once you acquire the taste
Iranians consider sweet drinks with food wrong — doogh is the answer
Bottled doogh is sold everywhere — but homemade is better
drinks.description: Iran's salty yogurt drink — fizzy, salty, minty, and the mandatory companion to every kabab. Iranians consider sweet drinks with meals wrong; doogh is the savory alternative. The 'salty fizzy yogurt?!' first-taste reaction and the mandatory kabab pairing make doogh viral.

drinks.name: Chai (Persian Tea)
instructions: Boil water in a kettle — place a small teapot on top to warm
Add loose tea to the small teapot — generous amount
Pour a small amount of boiling water over the tea — let it steep strongly
This concentrated tea (chay-e dam-kardeh) is the base
Pour a small amount of concentrate into a glass, dilute with hot water from the kettle
The color should be a deep ruby-red — not too light, not opaque
Place a sugar cube between your teeth and sip the tea THROUGH the sugar
This is 'drinking tea through sugar' — the traditional Iranian method
Tea is served in clear glasses so you can see the color — color matters
Iran is one of the world's top tea consumers — chai is constant and essential
drinks.description: Persian tea — strong black tea served in clear glasses (so you can judge the ruby color), sipped through a sugar cube held between the teeth. Iran is one of the world's highest per-capita tea consumers. The sugar-cube-through-teeth technique and the ruby-color standard are the most viral aspects of Iranian tea culture.

drinks.name: Sharbat-e Sekanjabin (Mint-Vinegar Drink)
instructions: Make syrup: boil sugar and water until dissolved
Add white vinegar — the sweet-sour balance is the art
Add fresh mint leaves — let steep as it cools
The result is a sweet-sour-minty syrup
Dilute with cold water or sparkling water to taste
Serve ice cold with fresh mint
Optionally, dip romaine lettuce leaves or cucumber in the syrup — an ancient serving method
Sekanjabin is over 2000 years old — one of the world's oldest recorded drinks
The lettuce-dipping method is uniquely ancient Persian
Sweet-sour-minty-cold is the most refreshing flavor combination
drinks.description: Iran's 2000-year-old vinegar-mint drink — a sweet-sour syrup diluted with cold water, one of the world's oldest recorded beverages. The ancient recipe (sugar, vinegar, mint) is unchanged from Sassanid-era Persia. The romaine-lettuce-dipping tradition and the 2000-year provenance are endlessly viral.

drinks.name: Ab-e Havij Bastani (Carrot Juice Float)
ingredients: Bastani sonnati (Iranian saffron ice cream) or vanilla ice cream
instructions: Juice fresh carrots — the juice should be thick and sweet
Pour into a tall glass
Add a large scoop of saffron ice cream on top — it floats
Dust with cinnamon
Drink/eat with a spoon and straw
The combination of sweet carrot juice and saffron ice cream is uniquely Iranian
This is Iran's juice-bar classic — every juice stand makes it
The orange-and-gold color combination is stunning
The ice cream melts into the carrot juice creating a creamy, saffron-carrot blend
drinks.description: Iran's juice-bar classic — fresh carrot juice with a scoop of saffron ice cream floating on top. The orange-and-gold color, the sweet-floral flavor blend, and the 'ice cream in juice?!' concept make this Iranian drink one of the most viral food mashups from the Middle East.
